title: One Record, Many Facts
content:
What problem does this solve?
Lists are good when position is meaningful. An expedition record contains named facts: destination, guide status, party, supplies, and clearance. A dictionary lets the program retrieve each fact by its label instead of memorizing a position. The intake desk still routes parties toward Gloamfen.

Previously in your program
Given supplies = ["rope", "torch"], which method adds "antidote" without replacing the list? Call supplies.append("antidote") — do not assign the return value back to supplies.

Basic syntax
  expedition = {
      "destination": "Gloamfen",
      "has_guide": True,
      "party": ["Mara", "Tovin", "Sable"],
      "supplies": ["rope", "torch", "antidote"]
  }
  expedition["status"] = "Cleared"
  print(expedition["destination"])

What actually happens
A dictionary stores key-value pairs. Keys are labels; values are the associated data. Retrieve with square brackets: record["destination"]. Change an existing value with assignment, or add a new key with the same syntax. A dictionary can contain lists as values. Contrast list indexing (party[0]) with dictionary lookup (record["party"]).

When this is useful
Use a dictionary when each piece of data has a meaningful name rather than only a position.
concepts: Look up and update values with record["key"]
Assignment can change an existing key or add a new one
Dictionary values can be lists or other data

examples.title: Field record
examples.explanation: Keys label each fact. status is added with assignment; destination and party are read by key.

common_mistakes: Looking up expedition[destination] without quotes around the key
Using parentheses instead of curly braces for the literal
Confusing = inside a dictionary literal with : between key and value
Assuming keys use numeric positions like a list

exercises.title: Read the record
exercises.prompt: What does this print? Type each line of output.
hints: Square brackets with a string key retrieve that value.
destination maps to the string Gloamfen; members maps to the integer 3.
Two print calls mean two lines: Gloamfen, then 3.

exercises.title: Quote the key
exercises.prompt: Python treats destination as a variable name and raises NameError. Retrieve the value using the dictionary’s string key.
hints: Dictionary keys that are text need quotes.
destination without quotes looks for a variable named destination.
Use record["destination"] so the key is the string destination.

tests.name: record
tests.message: Look up the value with record["destination"].

exercises.title: List or dictionary?
exercises.prompt: Which structure better represents one expedition with named facts such as destination, guide status, and clearance status?
choices: A list, because every value should be found by position
A dictionary, because each value has a meaningful label
A string, because the whole record can be one sentence
exercises.success_message: Exactly. The labels are part of the model, so dictionary keys make the record readable.
exercises.failure_message: Think about whether position or a named label best matches destination and clearance status.
hints: The facts already have names in English.
Lists shine when order is the main idea.

exercises.title: Create a field record
exercises.prompt:
Write make_record(destination, party, supplies) that returns a dictionary with exactly these keys:
- "destination"
- "party"
- "supplies"
- "member_count"

The value of "member_count" must be calculated with len(party), not hardcoded.
hints: Build a dictionary literal that stores the three inputs under matching keys.
member_count should call len on the party list.

exercises.title: Update clearance
exercises.prompt: Write set_clearance(record, status) that changes the record’s "status" value and returns the record. The key might be new or might already exist.
hints: Assignment with square brackets both updates and creates keys.
Write to record["status"], then return the same dictionary.
return the record after record["status"] = status.

exercises.title: Expedition Intake System v1
exercises.prompt:
Create build_expedition_record(destination, party, supplies, has_guide, warning_active).

It must:
1. Create a dictionary containing the original five inputs under keys "destination", "party", "supplies", "has_guide", and "warning_active".
2. Add "member_count" using len(party).
3. Add "supply_count" using len(supplies).
4. Add a "status" value:
   - "Denied" if there is no guide or a warning is active
   - otherwise "Cleared" for 5 or more supply items
   - otherwise "Review"
5. Return the completed dictionary.

Do not hardcode destinations, names, or counts.
exercises.starter_code:
def build_expedition_record(destination, party, supplies, has_guide, warning_active):
    # 1. Store the five inputs in a dictionary.
    # 2. Add member_count and supply_count with len.
    # 3. Set status: Denied if no guide or warning; else Cleared if supplies >= 5; else Review.
    # 4. Return the record.
    pass
exercises.success_message: Intake record complete. You combined decisions, Boolean logic, counting, collections, and functions into one program. In a damaged margin beside the old route, someone wrote: "Do not trust the statues."
hints: Build the dictionary from the inputs first. Then add calculated keys one at a time.
Check denial conditions before clearance. Either blocker should deny the expedition.
Use if not has_guide or warning_active, then elif len(supplies) >= 5, then else.

tests.message: Use if / elif / else to choose Denied, Cleared, or Review.
